### 2026-11-03: ## W5: Turing Machine

**8h**

## W5: Turing Machine
### Prototyping the circuit

For this week's project, I wanted to stick with the breadboard computer theme, and build my own 4-state Turing machine, capable of running small programs.

Instead of breadboards, I'm thinking I'll design a PCB and use JLC's PCBA to skip the time consuming soldering / wire cutting & placing I would have to do otherwise. This means I'll have to keep the parts I use simple to keep costs down.

As I only want to run small 4-state machine, I decided my user input will be entirely made of switches, rather than trying to get a small EEPROM to work. The 16 outputs will each have their own LED indicator for their value, as well as an additional LED indicating where the program head is. The head will wrap around the 16 bits, so I'll need to use shift registers.

Additionally, the clock speed can be controlled, or disabled to let the user manually step through the program.

With the plan out of the way, I booted up Seb Lague's `Digital-Logic-Sim` to wire up my circuit. I've had some experience with this tool before, but designing a full computer was much harder than I thought it'd be.

### Prototyping the circuit

I fully intend to redo the wiring in Logisim afterwards, but I thought doing a prototype in Digital-Logic-Sim would be a good way work out the key features I need.

I started by designing the clock pulse. On my PCB, the user should be able to choose how fast it goes, as well as whether the ticking is manual or automatic:

![Screenshot 2026-11-03 at 10.21.34](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/125d1dfb6284d581e5f0d2d797d1e21c79247b71fb86398cf7d77223a458cd9f.png)

I then designed a 4-bit shift register. It takes serial L and R data, so it can be chained, and you can choose which direction to shift in. An earlier version looked like this:

![Screenshot 2026-11-03 at 11.00.10](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/a34e6da6edb46b72db655e14df581da6dfd1c6528307e21ad08682a9d84eed37.png)

Chaining them together, we get 16-bit shifting.

![Screenshot 2026-11-03 at 11.11.59](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/12194bf6be52474924741cd8f69540818f6bc9653101abb56ea572c62f17c664.png)

I needed to add a 'reset' button however. Clearing the registers is easy, however setting the low bit afterwards took quite a lot of work. My solution in the end cleared the registers on the 'reset' buttons rising edge, and stored the bit on the falling edge:

![Screenshot 2026-11-03 at 12.26.00](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/5f67379bb15d834036d434d56eb3ccf30f5177a1542ddffb3620663ac71aa33f.png)

I then created the actual registers, which will store data on the tape. The head bit controls which position is read & written to.

![Screenshot 2026-11-03 at 17.51.43](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/32071312ce82927ef46e9f42d3bd4c4d65e515d5c524dc4256dfee7ed93567b4.png)

...and chained together:

![Screenshot 2026-11-03 at 12.49.19](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/873a86bf1af2fade6a45072ea3cfaf5aaa634adde6418f526042d33dc3b1a085.png)

 I then added the state information itself. On the PCB, these will simply be switches, however here I've used a small ROM. I needed to use lots of D-Latches to prevent any feedback loops, so the wiring did get quite messy.

![Screenshot 2026-11-03 at 14.47.57](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/a9fc8bcffad48ac41d156a5079587909f4303a235e2055371e95e33d67a062a3.png)

At this point, the computer is mostly done, however I found that the output was a bit inconsistent and wasn't giving the expected result. I found this to be the result of a few race conditions, as well as incorrect logic in my circuit.

After (somewhat) simplifying the circuit and removing unnecessary 'pulse' blocks, the machine finally works! I tested it by running the largest 'Busy Beaver' 4-state machine on it (search it up!), and exactly 107 steps later, the 'halt' flag was triggered and 13 LEDs were lit up in the output (the maximum!).

![Screenshot 2026-11-03 at 17.12.59](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/55c7469ab89eb3ddb6eb6e2f0ac8a226d709eeeda52a75eeb5e19086d4c1f3c0.png)

I still have some work to do massively simplifying the circuit, and getting rid of redundant logic gates.I intend to complete this in Logisim, before translating the circuit into real electronics in KiCad.

Thanks for reading!

### 2026-11-04: ## W5: Turing Machine

**8h**

## W5: Turing Machine
### Finalising the circuit in Logisim

This session was spent simplifying and polishing the circuit I previously made in Seb Lague's `Digital-Logic-Sim` program. I was new to Logisim and so this session took quite a lot of time to complete, however I'm very happy with the results.

I started by wiring the clock circuit:

![Screenshot 2026-11-03 at 19.22.57](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/7384763c8ed1a9893e0a0dc5041b4ca4d39419324e196fc6d888bde2285e447f.png)

I then added the first row of shift registers.

![Screenshot 2026-11-03 at 21.31.15](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/a26960d2c6fe5809779f6fec6a54a4209cad224a7ac81ce91622c4dcbe37812b.png)

At this point, I was still following my prototype circuit, and I was about to add another row of shifters. However, I realised that the design could be greatly simplified if I got rid of that second row - making the * tape * shift instead of the head.

I left this for the moment however, as I needed to work out the user input.

I decided on a 4 x 2 7-bit approach - 4 rows for each state, 2 columns for which bit was read, and 7 bits for which bit to right, which direction to move, and the remaining five will correspond to a slide switch that selects which state to transition into.

It came out a bit like this:

![Screenshot 2026-11-04 at 16.09.52](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/ff856add0f40df2611691a76cba95354f593844ba871b5f194273785e727584b.png)

The labels all connect up to these buses:

![Screenshot 2026-11-04 at 16.09.36](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/55b296f163a09be0621b18e84e7e5f49fa4e7cf206d8bee4b281a4a5ac305316.png)

I chose this approach as it would only require one multiplexer, rather than 7 which would be if I was to select each bit individually. However, I'm not 100% confident this setup will work with real electronics, so I will have to confirm this when I wire this up in KiCad.

At this point my circuit looked like the following. It was almost complete, however I still needed to add halting logic:

![Screenshot 2026-11-04 at 19.09.36](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/3407f02d3921fd4f3246cf8c6bf30a22fa257acc4a011eb0721234bf13fe6b7d.png)

I did this by using a chain of shift registers, although I did think this was somewhat wasteful:

![Screenshot 2026-11-04 at 21.28.17](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/ab3d0eb84cf6cf48c11c5af0ab8c716def4946bdc1e75bf320bfbb681147c4bc.png)

Putting it all together, I arrived at the following:

![Screenshot 2026-11-04 at 21.28.48](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/2904d9a3aa35063157214519fc2f6af6f66fe5be2a6ec56e542d48176bf47cf7.png)

I made a list of required parts for this design:

```
Required Parts:

7 x Shift Register (74194)

1 x Clock (555)

8 x Resistors (Pulldown)

8 x 5-Position Slide Switches
17 x 2-Position Slide Switches
2 x Button
2 x Pentiometer (Brightness Control, Clock Speed)

2 x 8-Bit LED Arrays
2 x LED (Clock, Halt)
         OR
18 x LED (Clock, Halt, Tape)

1 x Power Supply

1 x AND Gate
5 x NOT Gate
2 x OR Gate
4 x Tri-State-Buffer

1 x Demultiplexer
```

Much better than the first design, however, I felt there was still some simplification to be done.

It took quite a lot of work, however I managed to remove a good number of unnecessary logic gates, wires, and shift registers.

I arrived at the following:

![Screenshot 2026-11-04 at 22.18.43](https://halflife.hackclub-assets.com/sessions/3Z57nO3DOx0C7tgaKyZzjKBiZIWIGXGt/4517f09b63728641ea30b13b280dc976d2e24c67d2d7f0f5155e04da81768a53.png)

All thats left to do is wire it up in KiCad.

Thanks for reading!
